candidates.name: AWS native
candidates.role: S3 + managed PostgreSQL/pgvector or OpenSearch + Neptune + SQS/Step Functions/AWS Batch + CloudTrail/CloudWatch/KMS.
evidence: AWS recommends separate accounts for production and non-production workloads.
S3, Neptune, OpenSearch, and Batch have public service and pricing documentation.
S3 VPC gateway endpoints have no additional endpoint charge.
OpenSearch Serverless topology is mode-specific: the first Classic redundant collection in an account uses 2 OCU, Classic dev-test no-standby uses 1 OCU, and NextGen can configure minimum capacity 0.
limitations: Graph and vector/search are separate services with independent data, backup, ACL, and indexing behavior.

Classic redundant OpenSearch has a higher baseline than dev-test; NextGen scale-to-zero can introduce cold-wake latency. Subsequent collections may share OCUs depending on KMS key and collection topology.
Service APIs, IAM policies, and IaC are AWS-specific; exact region/SKU pricing must be refreshed.
candidates.reason: Broad native controls and operational cohesion fit the whole experiment flow; OpenSearch cost and cold-start tradeoffs depend on Classic redundant, dev-test no-standby, or NextGen scale-to-zero mode.

candidates.name: Google Cloud native
candidates.role: GCS + Spanner Enterprise Graph/Vector or Cloud SQL/AlloyDB + Pub/Sub/Workflows/Batch + Cloud Audit Logs/KMS.
evidence: Spanner Enterprise integrates relational, graph, full-text, and vector search features.
Spanner Graph and vector indexes require Enterprise or Enterprise Plus.
GCS Standard in Iowa is publicly listed at approximately USD 0.02 per GiB-month; Batch has no separate control-plane fee.
Base regional Spanner configurations have three read-write replicas; compute capacity is billed per replica, and granular 100 PU capacity is supported.
limitations: Spanner Graph uses GoogleSQL and is not available through the PostgreSQL interface.
Enterprise edition and replica/processing-unit choices set a cost floor.
GPU availability and quota vary by region and zone; Google-specific schemas reduce portability.

A 100 PU regional configuration is a three-replica topology; at the published Enterprise starting rate the compute-only arithmetic is about USD 89.79 per 730-hour month, before region-specific rates and other charges.
candidates.reason: The single Spanner Graph/Vector data plane aligns well with a source-linked KG, but Enterprise pricing and a non-PostgreSQL graph interface create cost and migration constraints.

candidates.name: Microsoft Azure native
candidates.role: Blob + PostgreSQL/pgvector + Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin + Azure AI Search + Service Bus/Azure Batch + Entra ID/Key Vault/Monitor.
evidence: Cosmos DB Gremlin is a managed graph API billed through throughput/query units.
Azure AI Search dedicated tiers bill per Search Unit; Azure Database for PostgreSQL supports pgvector.
Azure Batch itself has no service fee, while compute, storage, networking, and logs are billed.
limitations: Graph, vector/RAG, and relational stores remain separate; cross-store authorization and consistency are application responsibilities.
Cosmos Gremlin FAQ documents driver/protocol feature gaps; query compatibility must be tested.
Search Serverless Developer is currently preview without an SLA; Azure price depends on region, offer, and currency.
candidates.reason: Strong identity/private-network tools and supported vector database options are offset by separate graph/search services, tier/region-dependent costs, and Gremlin compatibility work.

candidates.name: Supabase PostgreSQL/pgvector + Neo4j AuraDB
candidates.role: Supabase stores canonical events/ACL-filtered vectors; Aura serves graph traversal; object artifacts remain in a separately selected cloud bucket.
evidence: Supabase supports pgvector and PostgreSQL Row Level Security.
Supabase Pro is listed at USD 25/month; Team starts at USD 599/month.
Aura Professional starts at USD 0.09 per GB-hour with a 1GB minimum; Business Critical/VDC tiers add enterprise controls.
limitations: No existing shared account, credential, corporate data, or project-specific access was granted.
Aura Professional pricing comparison excludes private endpoints and fine-grained RBAC/SSO; VPC isolation is a VDC tier condition.
Region co-location, private path, egress, ACL synchronization, account-level retention, and total cross-provider billing require SKU/contract review.
candidates.reason: Managed PostgreSQL/RLS and graph capability fit a quick whole-flow slice, but cross-provider network and authorization boundaries undermine operational simplicity until private tiers are verified.

candidates.name: Portable object + PostgreSQL/pgvector + Apache AGE + Temporal/Kubernetes
candidates.role: Keep source/artifact formats in a provider object store, use PostgreSQL/pgvector and Apache AGE for relational/vector/graph projections, and use Temporal/Kubernetes for portable jobs.
evidence: pgvector and Apache AGE are PostgreSQL extensions with public source and exportable SQL data models.
Temporal provides durable workflow primitives; Kubernetes schedules portable containers.
Apache AGE repository LICENSE is Apache-2.0; Temporal server repository LICENSE is MIT.
Provider-neutral object manifests, JSONL events, and pinned container images can reduce migration cost.
limitations: Self-hosted graph/query/runtime, database patching, upgrades, networking, backup, HA, IAM, and restore require an accountable operations team.
PostgreSQL graph extension behavior and scale must be evaluated against workload; portability does not guarantee equivalent performance.
Track transitive dependency licenses, notices, hosted Temporal Cloud contract, and Kubernetes distribution/support separately; no package was installed or approved.
candidates.reason: Highest control over export and provenance but requires much more day-2 ownership; Jev advisory favored this direction with only 0.46 confidence, not as a vendor decision.

candidates.name: Amazon Neptune
candidates.role: Managed AWS graph database for versioned design-point, hardware, kernel, and evidence relationships.
evidence: AWS publishes separate instance, storage, I/O, backup, and transfer billing dimensions.
Current pricing page includes an us-east-1 I/O-Optimized db.r5.large example at USD 0.4698/hour plus storage.
limitations: Instance and storage can dominate a small graph; selected region and Standard vs I/O-Optimized change cost.
Graph is separate from vector/search and canonical evidence stores.
Graph query/API semantics and export must be tested for the project schema.
candidates.reason: Managed graph and auditable billing dimensions fit the evidence graph, while always-on instance and multi-store costs limit low-volume economics.

candidates.name: Cloud Spanner Graph
candidates.role: Graph layer integrated with Spanner relational, full-text, and vector capabilities.
evidence: Graph nodes/edges are mapped from tables and queried through GQL-compatible interface.
Spanner Enterprise includes graph, full-text, and vector search; published starting compute price is per 100 processing units/hour/replica.
A base regional configuration has three read-write replicas; granular compute can be configured at 100 PU and pricing is per replica.
For a base regional instance, Google documents three read-write replicas; granular capacity can be configured at 100 PU and compute is billed per replica.
limitations: Enterprise or Enterprise Plus required; Spanner Graph is unavailable through PostgreSQL dialect.

A regional 100 PU capacity input bills across three read-write replicas; at the published Enterprise starting rate, USD 0.041 × (100/100) × 3 × 730h = about USD 89.79/month compute only. This is arithmetic, not a quote; selected region/edition, storage, backups, and network change the bill.
Spanner-specific schema/query requires a migration adapter for other graph stores.
candidates.reason: Integrated graph/vector/relational semantics suit evidence lineage, but edition floor and dialect lock-in are material.

candidates.name: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
candidates.role: Managed Gremlin graph projection for hardware composition, legality, and experiment lineage.
evidence: Fully managed Gremlin API; graph queries are billed based on RU/s consumed by objects and edges processed.
Supports horizontal partitioning and provisioned/autoscale/serverless billing models.
limitations: FAQ documents missing bytecode support and driver incompatibility for some newer Gremlin clients.
Partitioning/query pattern influences RU/s and query costs; a region-specific RU estimate requires an actual query profile.
Export to another graph dialect and point-in-time cross-store consistency need validation.
candidates.reason: Managed graph is viable if Gremlin compatibility matches the client, but RU behavior and protocol gaps need a representative test.

candidates.name: Neo4j AuraDB
candidates.role: Managed graph query projection for multilevel HW/kernel/workload/evidence relationships.
evidence: Aura is available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
Professional starts at USD 0.09/GB-hour (minimum 1GB); Business Critical starts at USD 0.20/GB-hour (minimum 2GB).
Business Critical pricing page lists multi-zone SLA, RBAC/SSO, IP filtering, and daily backups.
limitations: Professional excludes private endpoints, fine-grained RBAC/SSO, and SLA; higher features cost more.
VPC isolation/dedicated infrastructure and customer-managed keys are custom Virtual Dedicated Cloud conditions.
Actual cloud region, inter-service networking, backup retention, and egress need quote-level confirmation.
candidates.reason: Managed graph reduces operations and has useful enterprise tiers, but security/network requirements move the candidate above the published low-cost Professional tier.

candidates.name: Managed PostgreSQL + pgvector
candidates.role: Keep source metadata, ACL filters, event ledger, and vector projections in PostgreSQL; optionally attach a graph extension or separate graph store.
evidence: pgvector is supported by Supabase, AlloyDB, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL.
PostgreSQL RLS can enforce row-level access for vector retrieval.
Cloud SQL/PostgreSQL costs are largely compute, storage, backup, HA, and network dependent.
limitations: Vector index size, recall/latency, HNSW overhead, filtered-query behavior, and replica needs require measurements.
Postgres graph extensions do not automatically provide managed graph algorithms or graph-service operational semantics.
Managed PostgreSQL edition/extension allowlist and backup/export behavior vary by provider.
candidates.reason: Relational ACL plus vector data provides an exportable low-complexity baseline, with scale limits to be measured before larger corpus.

candidates.name: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
candidates.role: Managed hybrid lexical/vector retrieval and filtering.
evidence: Current us-east-1 pricing page example lists USD 0.24/OCU-hour and USD 0.02/GB-month managed storage.
The first Classic redundant collection in an account has a 2 OCU minimum total (1 indexing including primary+standby, 1 search including replica).
Classic dev-test without redundant standby has a 1 OCU minimum; NextGen collection groups can set minimum indexing and search capacity to 0.
limitations: At the us-east-1 example rate and 730 hours, the first Classic redundant collection minimum is USD 350.40/month before storage; dev-test no-standby is USD 175.20/month.
Subsequent collections may share OCUs subject to encryption key and collection topology; NextGen can scale to zero but has a 10–30 second wake latency.
Mode, collection type, selected region, data size, standby, and configured minimum alter actual cost and availability.
AWS-specific filtering/query configuration and private network pricing need confirmation.
candidates.reason: Managed hybrid retrieval remains useful; economics depend on selecting redundant Classic, dev-test no-standby, or NextGen scale-to-zero, each with a different availability and cold-start profile.

candidates.name: Spanner Vector Search
candidates.role: Vector retrieval colocated with relational/Spanner Graph data.
evidence: Supports ANN indexes and filters on stored/key columns.
Vector Search is part of Spanner Enterprise/Enterprise Plus capabilities.
limitations: Edition and provisioned processing-unit/replica charges apply even before query volume is known.
Index rebuild and quality tuning are workload dependent.
Spanner-specific schema and APIs increase migration work.
Regional compute is replicated to three read-write replicas and billed per replica; verify edition, 100 PU granularity, selected-region rate, and capacity before projecting a floor.
candidates.reason: Graph and vector colocation can simplify evidence joins, but Enterprise pricing and Spanner schema bind the platform.

candidates.name: Azure AI Search
candidates.role: Managed hybrid lexical/vector search with filters and index replicas/partitions.
evidence: Dedicated search bills by Search Units (replicas × partitions) and tier; serverless model is consumption based.
Current documentation identifies Serverless Developer as preview without SLA.
limitations: Dedicated SU capacity is billed hourly and can cost more than token embedding at low query rates.
Preview Serverless Developer is not production ready by SLA; region/feature limits can change.
Index export/rebuild and ACL filters must be proven with source-level permissions.
candidates.reason: Strong managed hybrid search and access-filter candidate; fixed tier floor or preview limitations need an explicit stage decision.

candidates.name: Provider-managed queue + workflow + Batch jobs
candidates.role: AWS SQS/Step Functions/Batch, GCP Pub/Sub/Workflows/Batch, or Azure Service Bus/Batch for durable run/step jobs.
evidence: AWS, GCP, and Azure Batch pages state no separate Batch control-plane fee; underlying VM/GPU/storage/network resources are billed.
GCP Pub/Sub charges by bytes, with the first 10 GiB/month basic-throughput allowance and published per-TiB pricing thereafter.
limitations: Queue, workflow, and job semantics differ by provider; portable event IDs/replay contract still required.
GPU instances, persistent disks, logs, NAT, and data transfer can dominate.
Provider quotas and regional GPU capacity can block jobs even when budget is available.
candidates.reason: Managed batch is the simplest execution boundary for reproducible job manifests, but job state and scheduler APIs are provider specific.

candidates.name: Temporal + Kubernetes jobs
candidates.role: Portable workflow history/retries with containerized CPU/GPU task workers and object-store artifacts.
evidence: Temporal provides durable workflow/event history; Kubernetes Jobs execute pinned containers.
Runtime and task containers can be redeployed on multiple cloud providers.
limitations: Control plane, worker pools, database, upgrades, HA, network policies, and capacity are customer-operated unless a managed service is selected.
Portable container does not make GPU availability, file semantics, secrets, or network costs portable.
Open-source license and hosted-service contract need separate legal review.
candidates.reason: Strong workflow portability and replay potential, but operational ownership is much higher than provider-managed Batch.

candidates.name: Hosted embedding API, online or batch
candidates.role: Metered API generates vectors for approved documents/query text without operating GPU workers.
evidence: OpenAI publishes per-million-input-token prices and a 50% Batch API discount; Vertex publishes online/batch input prices.
Current Vertex pricing table shows Gemini Embedding at USD 0.00015 per 1,000 count online and USD 0.00012 per 1,000 count batch, Global region.
API unit costs can be estimated from actual token/character counts before building GPU infrastructure.
limitations: Source content leaves the chosen cloud boundary; data residency, DPA, region, rate limits, and retention terms must be approved.
The visible Vertex price row says 1,000 count without defining the metered unit; do not convert that price to token envelopes until SKU usage billing confirms the unit.
Provider/model change may require re-embedding and index version migration.
Model relevance and retrieval quality require a separate domain evaluation; this candidate is infrastructure economics only.
candidates.reason: Good first infrastructure baseline because cost is directly metered and avoids GPU operations, subject to source privacy and provider contract.

candidates.name: Ephemeral batch GPU workers
candidates.role: Run a pinned embedding container on provider Batch/VM/GPU nodes and write vectors/artifacts into the selected private store.
evidence: AWS/GCP/Azure expose region/SKU pricing calculators; GPU node hours, disks, data egress, quotas, and capacity determine job cost.
GPU availability differs by provider region/zone; batch compute can be destroyed after completion.
limitations: No token-to-GPU-hour rate can be inferred without a model, hardware, batch shape, utilization, and approved benchmark.
Drivers, CUDA/toolchain, image supply chain, retries, preemption, and security patching become platform responsibilities.
Cost advantage requires measured all-in comparison against API metering; model quality is not assumed.
candidates.reason: Can keep source processing inside a private environment and control model/runtime versions, but economics and availability cannot be scored confidently yet.

candidates.name: Amazon S3
candidates.role: Versioned canonical source/artifact bucket, lifecycle/archive tiers, optional WORM retention.
evidence: S3 pricing separates storage, request/retrieval, transfer, replication, and management.
Object Lock supports WORM retention/legal hold; S3 gateway endpoints can privately reach S3 without extra endpoint charge.
limitations: Locked object versions cannot be deleted before retention; versioning/Object Lock must not conflict with legal deletion.
Standard storage rate is region dependent and must be pulled from current pricing calculator/price list.
S3 lifecycle and class minimum retention/retrieval charges need per-object policy review.
candidates.reason: Mature source/artifact storage with useful versioning and access controls; immutability and lifecycle charges need careful deletion policy.

candidates.name: Google Cloud Storage
candidates.role: Versioned canonical source/artifact object store with lifecycle and optional retention lock.
evidence: Current public standard rate in Iowa us-central1 is approximately USD 0.02/GiB-month with separate operations/egress.
Bucket Lock can permanently prevent reducing/removing a retention policy; Object Lifecycle Management supports tier and deletion policies.
limitations: Locked bucket policy is irreversible and can prevent bucket/project deletion until all objects expire.
Cross-region/dual-region placement changes storage and transfer pricing.
Object versioning increases stored-byte cost; lifecycle/delete behavior must align with retention.
candidates.reason: Clear regional storage price and retention/lifecycle tools make cost and evidence policy legible, with irreversible lock behavior as a governance gate.

candidates.name: Azure Blob Storage
candidates.role: Canonical source/artifact store with access tiers, versioning, lifecycle management, and optional immutability.
evidence: Storage tiers include hot/cool/cold/archive; charge depends on bytes, operations, redundancy, and transfer.
Immutable Blob supports time-based retention and legal holds; lifecycle rules can tier and expire eligible blobs.
limitations: Public page calculator may display dynamic offer/region-dependent rates rather than a single unit price.
Immutable blobs cannot be modified/deleted during retention; lifecycle delete does not override immutability.
Archive retrieval, redundancy and operation charges can outweigh low storage rates.
candidates.reason: Strong lifecycle and WORM features, but exact rates depend on account offer/region/redundancy and deletion restrictions.
